 The Best 2-Bay NAS for Backups, Plex, and Docker in 2026
Updated on

by Jim Mendenhall 
 Bottom line 
 The UGREEN DXP2800 is our pick for most homes that want a 2-bay NAS. It mirrors two drives, runs Plex or Jellyfin with hardware transcoding, and handles a few Docker apps. The GT version adds a 10GbE port for networks that can use it. If the NAS is mostly for backups, Synology’s more mature backup apps are worth the older hardware.
Recommendation
 The DXP2800 fits a home that wants Plex or a few Docker apps next to its backups. If you expect to outgrow one large drive within a few years, start with four bays instead.
 A 2-bay NAS holds two hard drives and, in nearly every home setup, mirrors them in RAID 1 so a dead drive does not take your files with it. That makes it an inexpensive way into network storage that survives a drive failure, and it is enough for phone photo backups, computer backups, and a family Plex or Jellyfin library. On most models, the only way to grow one is to replace both drives with larger ones. Our pick is the UGREEN DXP2800, and the table below lists the other 2-bay models worth buying in October 2026.

 The UGREEN DXP2800 costs $389.99, $30 more than Synology’s DS225+ at list price, and has newer hardware. Its Intel N100 is a four-core chip from 2023 with Intel Quick Sync, the video engine Plex and Jellyfin use to convert a 4K movie for a phone or an older TV without loading the CPU. It ships with 8GB of DDR5 on one SO-DIMM slot that takes a 16GB module, and it has two M.2 NVMe slots that work as an SSD cache for the hard drives or as a separate fast pool for Docker containers and photo thumbnails. UGOS Pro sits on a 32GB eMMC chip, so both bays stay free for data. UGREEN also allows TrueNAS or Unraid on the box and says a third-party system does not void the hardware warranty.
 The single 2.5GbE port has no upgrade path, since there is no PCIe slot. The M.2 slots sit behind both drive trays, so adding an SSD later means pulling the drives first. UGOS Pro has fewer apps than Synology’s DSM, and Plex and Jellyfin install as Docker containers rather than native packages. How-To Geek’s Andrew Heinzman, reviewing an early unit in 2024, recommended it to enthusiasts “but not first-time NAS users” , though UGREEN has added Docker and other missing features since. Packetswitch’s Suresh Vinasiththamby bought one with his own money, ran Pi-hole in Docker and an Ubuntu Server VM on it, and summed up the value as “the best bang for the buck.” 
 The DXP2800 GT brings 10GbE to two bays
 Two hard drives in a mirror cannot fill a 10GbE link, so the DXP2800 GT’s faster port pays off when you put SSDs in the M.2 slots or the bays, or when you edit video from the NAS over a 10GbE network. If your router and computers are 1GbE or 2.5GbE, the DXP2800 delivers the same speed for $70 less. UGREEN launched the GT in June 2026 with the same two bays and two M.2 slots, swapping the N100 for an AMD Ryzen Embedded R2514, a four-core, eight-thread chip with Radeon Vega graphics that transcode H.264 and H.265. Its one network port is 10GbE. Memory is 8GB of DDR4 expandable to 64GB. UGREEN’s manual lists ECC SO-DIMMs as supported, as on the four-bay DXP4800 GT , though the module in the box is not ECC. UGREEN’s store sells it for $459.99.
 Idle power is the GT’s main drawback. In Notebookcheck’s October 2026 review , it drew 14.84 to 20.14 W at idle with two hard drives spinning, and the reviewer listed “relatively high idle power consumption” and “no volume encryption” among its cons, next to “quiet operation” and “expandable RAM” among the pros. Every 10 W of continuous draw adds about 88 kWh a year, roughly $16 at a US average rate of about 18 cents per kWh.
 The TerraMaster F2-425 Plus adds 5GbE ports for $110 more
 Each of the TerraMaster F2-425 Plus’s two 5GbE ports carries twice the speed of the DXP2800’s port, and its third M.2 slot leaves room for an SSD pool plus a cache. It lists at $499.99 on TerraMaster’s US store (it launched at $399.99) and runs an Intel N150 (a slightly faster successor to the N100, also with Quick Sync) with 8GB of DDR5 that goes to 32GB. It runs TOS 6, TerraMaster’s own system, which covers backups, photo sync, and Docker.
 Each M.2 slot runs at PCIe 3.0 x1, according to Liliputing’s coverage of the launch , which caps an SSD at about 1GB/s. That is still faster than a 5GbE port can carry, so files served over the network lose nothing, but apps and VMs running on the NAS itself cannot use full NVMe speed. TOS has a smaller community than DSM or UGOS Pro, which means fewer guides when something goes wrong. The TerraMaster F4-425 Plus puts the same chip and ports in four bays with 16GB of memory.
 A Synology DS225+ or DS725+ fits a backup-first home
 DSM’s Hyper Backup, Active Backup for Business, Synology Photos, and Snapshot Replication are more mature than the equivalents on UGOS Pro or TOS, and they need little attention once set up. On two drives, Synology Hybrid RAID behaves like a mirror. The UGREEN vs Synology comparison covers the software gap in detail.
 The Synology DS225+ launched in July 2025 and lists at $360, but it runs DSM on a Celeron J4125 from 2019. Memory starts at 2GB and tops out at 6GB, and without M.2 slots there is no room for an SSD cache or app pool. Networking is one 2.5GbE port plus a 1GbE port. Its Intel graphics have Quick Sync, but hardware transcoding does not work on stock DSM. In a Plex forum thread on the DS425+ , which uses the same chip, a Plex engineer wrote in August 2025 that he had “removed all X25+ products from Hardware Transcoding Support,” a DS225+ owner reported the same problem on Jellyfin, and later posts in the thread point owners to a community-written script that turns it on. Dong Knows Tech called the DS225+ “an excellent compact NAS server for those needing modest network-attached storage space” . It works better as a backup appliance than as a media or app server.
 The DS725+ can grow past two bays, because Synology’s DX525 expansion unit adds five more. It moves to an AMD Ryzen R1600 with 4GB of ECC memory (32GB at most) and two M.2 slots. The R1600 has no graphics engine, so Plex streams only files your devices can play as they are. It also has no route to 10GbE, which TechRadar’s review called “a shocking choice” for Synology to make.
 At launch, the 2025 Plus models accepted only Synology-branded or Synology-approved drives. DSM 7.3, released in October 2025, lifted that rule for third-party SATA hard drives and SSDs. M.2 storage pools on the DS725+ still need SSDs from Synology’s compatibility list.
 The UGREEN DH2300 handles backups but not Docker
 UGREEN’s store sells the DH2300 for $239.99, the lowest price here. Its eight-core Rockchip RK3576 is an ARM chip, the 4GB of memory is soldered, and the single network port runs at 1GbE. Its version of UGOS also has no official Docker support, which Mighty Gadget’s review said “severely restricts functionality that many people want from a NAS.” It still mirrors two drives, backs up phones and computers, and serves files to a TV. The DXP2800 costs $150 more and adds Docker, hardware transcoding, 2.5GbE, and two M.2 slots.
 Two drives in RAID 1 give you the space of one
 In RAID 1, every file lands on both drives, and the NAS keeps running if either one dies. RAID 0 stripes data across both for the full capacity and more speed, but one failed drive loses everything on both. JBOD or Basic volumes treat the drives as separate disks with no protection. For a home NAS that holds family photos and backups, RAID 1 is the setting to use.

 Formatted space shows up a little lower than the label, because drive makers count a terabyte as 1,000 gigabytes while Windows counts 1,024. Buy the pair larger than you think you need: growing a 2-bay mirror means buying two new drives, replacing one at a time, and waiting for the NAS to rebuild after each swap. A pair of large NAS drives can cost as much as the NAS itself, so price the drives before you compare enclosures.
 RAID 1 protects against a dead drive and nothing else. A deleted folder, ransomware, or a house fire takes both copies at once. Keep a second copy on a USB drive, a second NAS, or cloud storage, and turn on snapshots if your NAS supports them.
 CMR NAS drives hold up during a rebuild
 Use drives sold for NAS duty, such as Seagate IronWolf or WD Red Plus, rather than cheap desktop drives. Most NAS drives use conventional magnetic recording (CMR), while some low-cost drives use shingled magnetic recording (SMR), which slows down badly during long sustained writes. A RAID rebuild is exactly that kind of write. In 2020, after owners found that some 2TB to 6TB WD Red drives used SMR and struggled with rebuilds, WD split the line : plain WD Red became the SMR range, and WD Red Plus became the CMR range for NAS use. Check the maker’s spec sheet for “CMR” before you buy.
 Two spinning drives in a small box are audible in a quiet room, especially while the NAS scrubs or indexes photos, so a closet, office, or media shelf suits a 2-bay NAS better than a bedroom. If you can, buy the two drives from different retailers or batches, which lowers the chance that one manufacturing fault reaches both halves of the mirror.
 Four bays leave room to grow
 Close modal 
 A four-bay NAS costs more up front. With four drives in RAID 5, you lose one drive to protection instead of half, so four 12TB drives give you about 36TB usable, against 12TB from a mirrored pair. You can also start with two drives and add the other two later, which a 2-bay box cannot do. If your photo and video library is already past a few terabytes, or you plan to rip a disc collection into Plex, start at four bays.
 UGREEN’s four-bay step up is the UGREEN DXP4800 Plus , with a Pentium Gold 8505, a 10GbE port plus a 2.5GbE port, and memory to 64GB. On the Synology side, the Synology DS925+ keeps DSM’s backup apps but has no hardware transcoding, and the NAS comparison chart lists every other four-bay model.
 A mini PC can replace a 2-bay NAS for flash storage
 With SSDs instead of hard drives, a mini PC runs quieter than any NAS full of spinning drives. The Beelink ME Mini is a small cube that runs TrueNAS, Unraid, or Proxmox, with six M.2 slots, an Intel N150, and two 2.5GbE ports. Flash costs far more per terabyte than hard drives, so this route suits a few terabytes of fast storage, not a large media library. Our guide to using a mini PC as a NAS compares the two routes, and the 10GbE mini PC NAS guide covers faster networking from the mini PC side.
 Check your network speed before you choose
 A NAS moves files only as fast as the slowest link between it and your computer. Your router’s admin page lists the speed of each wired port, and your computer’s network settings show its own link speed. If either one reads 1 Gbps, a 2.5GbE port on the NAS runs at 1GbE too, and the extra money for the DXP2800 GT’s 10GbE or the TerraMaster’s 5GbE ports buys nothing until the switch and computers are upgraded.

 Who a 2-bay NAS is for
 A 2-bay NAS is the entry point to home storage and suits people whose main goals are backups and a private photo cloud. With two drives you can run a mirror, where the same data is written to both disks, so if one fails the other keeps your files safe while you replace it. The trade-off is capacity: a mirror gives you only half the raw storage, because the second drive is a copy rather than extra space.
 That makes a 2-bay ideal for phone photo backup, document storage and syncing files between devices, and acceptable for light media streaming if you pick an Intel model. It is less suited to a fast-growing Plex library or a home lab, where the limited bay count means you run out of room sooner and have fewer options for redundancy.

 Frequently asked questions
 Why does a 2-bay only give me half the storage?
 In a mirror, the second drive holds an identical copy of the first so your data survives a single drive failure. That protection costs capacity: two four-terabyte drives give four terabytes usable, not eight. If you want more usable space and redundancy together, step up to a 4-bay.
 Can I run Plex on a 2-bay NAS?
 An Intel 2-bay such as the DXP2800, DS224+ or TS-264 runs Plex and handles direct play and light transcoding fine. ARM models like the DH2300 and TS-233 can serve Plex for direct play but struggle to transcode, so avoid them if your TVs or phones need on-the-fly conversion.
 Should I run two drives as a mirror or as one big volume?
 Most home users should mirror, so a single drive failure does not lose data. Combining both drives into one large non-redundant volume gives more space but no protection, which is risky for irreplaceable photos. Only do that if you have a solid separate backup.
 Do the M.2 NVMe slots on a 2-bay help?
 On models like the DXP2800 and TS-264 the NVMe slots can act as a fast cache or, on some platforms, a separate fast pool. For a basic backup and photo workload they are a nice extra rather than essential, but they are useful if you later run more demanding apps.
 Is a 2-bay enough to last me a few years?
 If your needs are backups, documents and a phone photo cloud, yes. If you expect a large media library or a home lab, you may outgrow two bays sooner than you think, and a 4-bay gives far more room and redundancy options for not a great deal more money once drives are counted.

HDMI output lets you connect it directly to a display, and NFC makes pairing a phone quick.

Memory is fixed, networking is a single gigabit port, and UGOS Pro, UGREEN’s NAS operating system, is the youngest OS in this guide, with fewer community guides than QTS or ADM.
 If the goal is a file server and photo backup target with 4 GB of memory, the DH2300 is the buy. If you need containers, look at the TS-233 or AS3302T below; for a media server, keep compute on a separate mini PC.
 Best 2.5GbE Under $300: ASUSTOR Drivestor 2 Pro Gen2
 The ASUSTOR Drivestor 2 Pro Gen2 (AS3302T v2) is the only pick in this guide with a 2.5GbE port, and it usually costs roughly $280. If your switch and computers support 2.5GbE, it lifts large transfers well beyond the gigabit ceiling of the other two.
 CPU: Realtek RTD1619B, 4-core ARM64, 1.7 GHz
 Memory: 2 GB DDR4, not expandable
 Storage: 2x 3.5”/2.5” SATA bays
 Network and ports: 1x 2.5GbE, 3x USB 3.2 Gen 1
 Rated power: 13.1W in operation, 4.5W with disks hibernating (ASUSTOR)
 2.5GbE raises the ceiling for large sequential transfers from about 112 MB/s on gigabit to roughly 280 MB/s. For video projects, photo library syncs, and full-system restores, the difference is immediately useful.
 ADM (ASUSTOR Data Master) is a capable NAS OS with a clean interface and regular updates. App Central offers Docker Engine and Portainer CE for ARM64 models including this one (ADM 4.3 or later), so a few light containers are possible within 2 GB of memory. Three USB 3.2 ports give you room for external drives, a UPS connection, or USB dongles, and a built-in AES-256 engine handles encrypted shared folders without loading the CPU.
 The limits are the RTD1619B’s modest cores and the fixed 2 GB: no Plex hardware transcoding and no VMs. It costs about $60 more than the TS-233, a fair trade if your network supports 2.5GbE. If you’re still on gigabit, the TS-233 or DH2300 is better value. As with any NAS, keep ADM updated and don’t expose it directly to the internet.
 Budget Pick: QNAP TS-233
 The QNAP TS-233 is the least expensive pick at roughly $220, and it runs QTS, a mature, actively maintained NAS OS with a real app ecosystem.
 CPU: ARM Cortex-A55, 4 cores, 2.0 GHz
 Memory: 2 GB on board, not expandable
 Storage: 2x 3.5”/2.5” SATA bays
 Network and ports: 1x 1GbE, 1x USB 3.2 Gen 1, 2x USB 2.0
 Rated power: 10.8W typical with drives installed, 3.4W in disk standby (QNAP)
 At this price, calibrate expectations. The TS-233 is an excellent file server and backup target: SMB and NFS shares, scheduled backups to USB drives, and Hybrid Backup Sync for other NAS units and cloud storage. QNAP lists volume snapshots for basic data protection. Indexing a large photo library will be slow on 2 GB, but it works.
 Container Station is supported too. QNAP lists Docker and LXD support on the TS-233, with at least 1 GB of RAM required, so a few ARM64 containers are realistic as long as you keep the stack light. Its four Cortex-A55 cores run at 2.0 GHz, versus 1.7 GHz on the ASUSTOR’s RTD1619B.
 QNAP rates the TS-233 at about 10.8W in typical operation with drives installed. At $0.18 per kWh, that is about $17 a year running around the clock, and less when the disks spin down.
 The limits: no Plex hardware transcoding, no Virtualization Station, 2 GB of memory on the board, a single gigabit port, and one USB 3.2 port for expansion. If you need a reliable file server and backup appliance at the lowest practical price, the TS-233 delivers. Keep QTS updated, since QNAP’s security record calls for prompt patching.
 How to Choose: Buying Criteria
 ARM Workload Boundaries
 Every pick here uses an ARM processor. That keeps price and power low, but it sets clear limits:
 Best for file serving, backup, and direct-play media
 ARM64 containers only, on the QNAP and ASUSTOR, and none officially on the UGREEN
 No Plex hardware transcoding
 No practical virtual machines
 Low vendor-rated power, about 10 to 13W in operation
 If your NAS is purely a file server and backup target, these models save money and power. If Docker at scale, VMs, or Plex transcoding are requirements, use our full NAS comparison and raise the hardware budget.
 RAM: The Hidden Bottleneck
 Memory is fixed in every pick, so buy enough for the appliance’s lifetime:
 NAS Ships With Expandable? 
 UGREEN DH2300 4 GB No 
 ASUSTOR AS3302T v2 2 GB No 
 QNAP TS-233 2 GB No 
 The UGREEN’s 4 GB is comfortable for file serving and basic apps. The 2 GB models are tight but workable for their intended use.
 Networking: 1GbE vs 2.5GbE
 At this price, you’re choosing between 1GbE (about 112 MB/s) and 2.5GbE (about 280 MB/s). The practical impact depends on the workload:
 Small file transfers (documents, code repos): No difference. Both feel instant.
 Large file transfers (video, photos, backups): 2.5GbE cuts wait times by about 60%. A 50 GB backup takes about 7.5 minutes on 1GbE and about 3 minutes on 2.5GbE.
 Media streaming : Even 4K HDR remuxes (80+ Mbps) fit well within 1GbE, so you don’t need 2.5GbE for streaming.
 Multi-client access : 1GbE becomes a bottleneck sooner when several users hit the NAS at once.
 The ASUSTOR AS3302T v2 has 2.5GbE; the other two are 1GbE. If you regularly move large files and your network supports 2.5GbE, the improvement is worth paying for.
 Software Ecosystem: QTS vs ADM vs UGOS
 QNAP QTS (TS-233): Feature-rich but more complex. Container Station works on the TS-233 for light ARM64 containers. QNAP’s security history is weaker, so keep auto-update enabled.
 ASUSTOR ADM (AS3302T v2): Clean, capable, regularly updated. Docker Engine and Portainer CE are available in App Central. The app library and community are smaller than DSM’s or QTS’s.
 UGREEN UGOS Pro (DH2300): The newest platform, with a modern mobile app and strong photo backup. No official Docker support on this model, and the smallest third-party ecosystem.
 Bottom Line
 For the most hardware for file storage, the UGREEN DH2300 delivers an 8-core CPU and 4 GB of RAM at a $269.99 list price. Just don’t buy it for Docker or a Plex server.
 If 2.5GbE matters, the ASUSTOR AS3302T v2 is the only pick here with it, and it runs light ARM64 containers through Portainer CE.
 For the lowest price, the QNAP TS-233 runs QTS with Container Station, gets regular security updates, and has a low vendor-rated power draw.
 Ready to see what a bigger budget gets you? Our full NAS comparison covers 4-bay models and beyond.
 Frequently Asked Questions
 What is the best NAS under $300? The UGREEN DH2300, listed by UGREEN at $269.99, offers the most CPU cores and memory for file storage and photo backup. Choose the ASUSTOR AS3302T v2 (roughly $280) when 2.5GbE matters, or the QNAP TS-233 (roughly $220) when you want the lowest price and Docker support.
 Can you run Docker on a cheap NAS? Yes, within limits. The QNAP TS-233 runs Docker through Container Station, and the ASUSTOR AS3302T v2 offers Docker Engine and Portainer CE, both for ARM64 images. With 2 GB of memory, plan for a few light services. The UGREEN DH2300 does not officially support Docker. For broad Docker use, budget for an x86 model with more memory.
 Is an ARM NAS worth buying in 2026? Yes, if your needs are file storage, backup, and photo sync. ARM NAS units like the QNAP TS-233 and UGREEN DH2300 are efficient always-on file servers. They fall short for heavy Docker use, Plex hardware transcoding, and virtual machines.
 Which NAS under $300 has 2.5GbE? In this guide, the ASUSTOR Drivestor 2 Pro Gen2 (AS3302T v2). The other picks use 1GbE, which is enough for backups and basic file serving but caps a single transfer near 112 MB/s.
 How much RAM does a budget NAS need? 2 GB is adequate for simple file serving and scheduled backups. 4 GB gives more headroom for indexing, photo apps, and several users. Memory is fixed in all three picks, so choose the UGREEN DH2300 if the extra headroom matters and you don't need Docker.

 You don't need to spend $500 on a NAS enclosure. The best budget NAS devices deliver 2.5G Ethernet, solid backup software, and reliable 24/7 operation for under $300 — drives sold separately.
 Budget NAS devices have improved dramatically over the past few years. Where $200-$300 once bought a slow ARM chip with 512MB of RAM and basic file-sharing support, that same price range now covers dual-core and quad-core ARM processors, Intel N95 and N100 efficiency chips, 2.5G Ethernet ports, and mature software ecosystems. You can build a very capable home NAS without approaching the $500-$700 range that four-bay and performance-focused units occupy.
 This guide focuses exclusively on enclosure prices. Drives are sold separately for all of these units, and that cost deserves its own section below.

 What You Actually Get Under $300: Managing Expectations
 Under $300, the tradeoffs are predictable and manageable once you know what they are.
 Two bays only. Every NAS in this price range is a 2-bay device. That means a maximum of two hard drives, which is enough for RAID 1 mirroring or JBOD (Just a Bunch of Disks) for maximum capacity. If you need four or more bays for a large media library or RAID 5, you are looking at a different price tier.
 1GbE is still common at the low end. The TerraMaster F2-424 and UGREEN DXP2800 stand out by offering 2.5G Ethernet at around $250-$280. The Synology DS223, QNAP TS-233, and TerraMaster F2-212 all ship with standard gigabit Ethernet, which is sufficient for most backup and file-sharing tasks but limits peak transfer speeds to roughly 100-110 MB/s.
 ARM vs Intel CPUs. Three of the five picks here use ARM Cortex-A55 processors. These are efficient, quiet, and handle file sharing, Time Machine, and rsync backups without breaking a sweat. They cannot do hardware video transcoding, and Docker container support is limited. The Intel N95 and N100 chips in the TerraMaster F2-424 and UGREEN DXP2800 change the equation: Intel Quick Sync handles hardware transcoding, and Docker works well.
 RAM is typically 2-4GB and often not expandable. Budget units ship with 2GB DDR4 in most cases. That is fine for file serving and backups, but heavier workloads like simultaneous Docker containers or running VMs require more RAM, which often means stepping up to a different model.
 ARM vs Intel CPU in a Budget NAS: What It Means for You
 The CPU difference in a NAS matters more than the brand on the case. Here is the practical breakdown.
 ARM Cortex-A55 (Synology DS223, QNAP TS-233, TerraMaster F2-212): These processors are power-efficient and perfectly adequate for the primary NAS use cases: Samba file sharing, Time Machine backups, Windows File History via SMB, rsync jobs, and photo storage. Synology's Moments and Photos apps run fine on the DS223. The limitation is transcoding — streaming a video to a device that cannot direct play the format requires software transcoding, which is slow and limits you to one stream at modest quality.
 Intel N95 / N100 (TerraMaster F2-424, UGREEN NASync DXP2800): Intel's Alder Lake N-series efficiency processors bring a major upgrade. Intel Quick Sync hardware transcoding handles 4K H.264 and H.265 decoding, which is a real difference for Plex or Jellyfin users. Docker containers for applications like Home Assistant, AdGuard Home, or Nextcloud run much more reliably. For around $250-$280, the TerraMaster F2-424 and UGREEN DXP2800 offer capabilities that traditionally lived in the $400+ tier.
 2.5G Ethernet at $250: Is the TerraMaster F2-424 Worth It Over Synology?
 The TerraMaster F2-424 costs about $50 more than the Synology DS223 and brings two meaningful upgrades: a 2.5G Ethernet port and an Intel N95 processor. The Synology DS223 sticks with 1GbE and an ARM chip but runs DSM 7 — arguably the best NAS software available.
 In practice, this comes down to your priorities. The TerraMaster F2-424 wins on hardware per dollar. Intel hardware transcoding, 2.5G network throughput (up to ~280 MB/s when paired with a 2.5G switch and compatible computer), and better Docker support make it the performance leader in this price bracket. TOS (TerraMaster Operating System) has improved but still lags DSM in app ecosystem depth and polish.
 The Synology DS223 wins on software. DSM 7 is mature, regularly updated, has a deep app ecosystem (Hyper Backup, Surveillance Station, Drive, Photos, Moments), and is the easiest NAS to manage for non-technical users. If long-term reliability, software quality, and ease of use matter most, the DS223 is worth the hardware compromise.
 The Real Cost: Budget NAS Enclosure Plus Drives
 The enclosure price is only part of what you will spend. A NAS without drives is a box. Here is the realistic total-cost math.
 A pair of 8TB Seagate IronWolf NAS drives typically costs $160-$180 each, putting the drive pair at $320-$360. Add the enclosure cost:
 TerraMaster F2-424 (~$250) + 2x8TB IronWolf: Total system cost roughly $570-$610
 UGREEN DXP2800 (~$280) + 2x8TB IronWolf: Total system cost roughly $600-$640
 Synology DS223 (~$200) + 2x8TB IronWolf: Total system cost roughly $520-$560
 For comparison, a Synology DS224+ (the Intel-based upgrade from the DS223) at around $300 plus the same drives lands at $620-$660 — only $50-$100 more than the DS223 build, but with a meaningful CPU upgrade and 2GB more RAM. If you are near the DS223 option, it is worth pricing out the DS224+ before committing.
 If budget is a hard ceiling and you just need reliable home backups with modest capacity, 4TB drives cut the drive cost roughly in half. Two 4TB IronWolf drives run $70-$90 each, bringing total system cost for a DS223 build to around $340-$380.
 Setting Up a Budget NAS for the First Time: What to Expect From TOS and QTS Lite
 Synology's DSM 7 is widely considered the gold standard for NAS software. Initial setup involves connecting the NAS to your router, opening a browser to find.synology.com, and following a straightforward wizard. Time Machine and Windows File History are configured from the control panel, and shared folders are accessible from any device on the network within minutes of first boot.
 TerraMaster's TOS (TerraMaster Operating System) has evolved considerably and now supports most core NAS functions: shared folders, user accounts, RAID management, Docker, and a growing app store. The interface is less polished than DSM and the app library is smaller, but it covers everything most home users need. TOS setup follows a similar browser-based wizard process.
 QNAP's QTS is feature-rich but sometimes overwhelming. QNAP builds in many security features and advanced networking options that DSM makes optional. For a first NAS, QTS takes slightly more time to configure correctly — particularly around disabling unnecessary remote access features and setting up proper user accounts. The payoff is flexibility: QTS supports a wide range of apps and containers.
 UGREEN's UGOS (UGREEN OS) is the newest software platform on this list. It has improved rapidly and covers the basics well, but the app ecosystem is still developing compared to Synology and QNAP.
 Frequently Asked Questions
 Is a $200 NAS good enough for home backups?
 Yes — even an ARM-based NAS handles Time Machine, Windows File History, and rsync reliably for a household. The Synology DS223 at around $200 runs full DSM 7 and has excellent app support for backup workflows. You will not feel constrained for standard backup use cases.
 Can a budget NAS run Plex?
 Only reliably with direct play. Software transcoding on ARM or low-end Intel CPUs is limited to 1-2 streams at modest quality. If you need reliable transcoding, the TerraMaster F2-424 or UGREEN DXP2800 with Intel N95/N100 offer hardware transcoding via Intel Quick Sync, which handles 4K H.264 and H.265 decoding. ARM-based picks like the DS223 are better suited to direct-play Plex setups where client devices handle decoding themselves.
 What is the difference between the Synology DS223 and DS224+?
 The DS224+ uses an Intel Celeron J4125 with faster performance, hardware transcoding, and 2GB of RAM expandable to 6GB. The DS223 uses an ARM-based Realtek RTD1619B with lower power draw and a lower price. Both run DSM 7 with the full Synology software ecosystem. The DS224+ handles heavier workloads — transcoding, multiple simultaneous users, Docker containers — significantly better than the DS223.
 Do budget NAS devices support RAID?
 Yes — all NAS devices on this list support RAID 0, RAID 1, and JBOD. RAID 1 mirrors your data across both drives for redundancy, meaning you keep working if one drive fails. RAID 0 stripes data across both drives for faster performance but no redundancy. JBOD presents both drives as separate volumes. Remember that RAID is not a backup — it only protects against a single drive failure, not accidental deletion, fire, theft, or ransomware.

A backup-only box can be a cheap ARM unit that sips power. A media server needs an Intel chip with Quick Sync, and the cheapest models skip it.
 Original content from computingforgeeks.com - post 177134 
 We compared six current 2-bay models from Synology, UGREEN and TerraMaster for three kinds of buyer. You want automatic backups of phones and laptops, you want a Plex or Jellyfin server, or you’ve never owned a NAS and want the fewest surprises. Each pick is priced with a mirrored pair of CMR drives, since two drives in RAID 1 give you the capacity of one. This is desk research from vendor spec sheets and cited reviews, not a bench test, and prices and stock below were checked on Amazon on October 24, 2026.
 Best 2-bay NAS picks at a glance
 Start from what the NAS will do for you, not from the spec sheet. Each award below names the job it is best at:
 Best for first-time owners: Synology DS225+ , about $365. DSM is the easiest NAS software to live with, and it carries a three-year warranty.
 Best for Plex and Jellyfin: UGREEN DXP2800 , about $390. An Intel N100 with Quick Sync, 8 GB of DDR5 and two M.2 slots.
 Best budget x86 box: TerraMaster F2-425 , about $255. Quick Sync and 2.5GbE for the price of an ARM box, with a locked OS.
 Best premium pick: UGREEN DXP2800 GT , about $460. The only 10GbE port in this guide and room for 64 GB of RAM.
 Cheapest box for backups: Synology DS223j , about $210. DSM backup tools on a 1 GB ARM box with one gigabit port.
 Lowest power draw: UGREEN DH2300 , about $239. Rated 13.72 W while working, but no Docker and no Plex server.
 Prices move daily, so treat these as the level we saw and check the live listing before you buy. If the box will ever run a media server, skip straight to the DXP2800 or the F2-425, because the two ARM picks and the DS225+ cannot transcode for Plex as shipped.
 How we picked these six
 Every spec in this guide comes from the maker’s own product page, and every price and stock line from Amazon’s catalog API on October 24, 2026. We only kept NAS listings sold by Amazon.com or the brand’s own Amazon storefront, so a warranty claim goes to someone accountable. Speeds, idle power and noise come from the independent reviews linked in each section. We did not bench these units ourselves, and where we found no independent test, we say so.
 We left out boxes we could not verify or buy cleanly, and there is a short list of those near the end. If you’d rather build than buy, our DIY NAS on a mini PC guide prices that route against these boxes.
 2-bay NAS comparison table
 These columns hold the specs that change the decision for a 2-bay buyer. Quick Sync decides Plex, the network port decides copy speed, and the warranty and OS rules decide what happens in year three:

 Read the Quick Sync column first. Three boxes have it, and only two of those use it for Plex without extra work, which is why the DS225+ wins for first-time owners but not for media servers. The 1GbE boxes top out near 115 MB/s on copies, so copying 10 TB onto one takes about a day. The 2.5GbE boxes need roughly 10 to 15 hours, depending on how fast each writes.
 Mirrored drives cost more than the box
 A 2-bay NAS almost always runs RAID 1, which writes every file to both drives, so you pay for two drives and get the space of one. That makes the drives the bigger bill. These are the cheapest new CMR NAS drives we found sold by Amazon.com (Adorama for the 6TB), priced as a mirrored pair:
 Drive Price each on Oct 24, 2026 Mirrored pair Usable space Per usable TB 
 WD Red Plus 6TB (sold by Adorama) $299.99 $599.98 6 TB $100.00 
 WD Red Plus 10TB $459.99 $919.98 10 TB $92.00 
 WD Red Pro 12TB $539.99 $1,079.98 12 TB $90.00 
 WD Red Pro 16TB $714.99 $1,429.98 16 TB $89.37 
 WD Red Pro 20TB $907.47 $1,814.94 20 TB $90.75 
 From 10 TB up, the cost per usable TB barely moves, between $89 and $92, so buy the largest pair you can afford now. Two bays cannot grow by adding a third drive. The only upgrade path is replacing both drives with bigger ones, one at a time, with a full rebuild after each swap. The 6TB pair is the worst value per TB here, and it was the smallest new CMR drive we found from a seller we’d trust. No 4TB or 8TB CMR drive was sold by Amazon.com when we checked.
 With a 10TB pair, the full builds land between about $1,130 (DS223j) and $1,380 (DXP2800 GT), which is why a cheaper box rarely changes the total by much. Buy CMR drives only, since SMR drives can stall a rebuild for days. The CMR vs SMR explainer covers why, and our NAS hard drive rankings track more sizes and brands by price per TB.
 1. Synology DS225+
 For someone who has never owned a NAS, the DS225+ is the 2-bay box we’d hand over first. DSM’s backup apps, snapshots and phone photo backup are the most finished software in this guide, and Synology is the only maker here that gives three years of warranty.
 Synology DS225+: Celeron J4125, 1GbE plus 2.5GbE, three-year warranty. Image: Synology. 
 Inside is a four-core Celeron J4125 with 2 GB of DDR4, expandable to 6 GB, two hot-swap bays for up to 48 TB raw, and one 1GbE plus one 2.5GbE port. Synology rates it at 282 MB/s reads, and NASCompares reports up to 280 to 290 MB/s over 2.5GbE, so the faster port is real. Synology rates writes lower, at 217 MB/s. That review also found DSM using 28 to 38% of the RAM at rest, which is the first sign that 2 GB is tight once you add apps.
 The 2025 drive lock is gone too, and that was the big complaint when this model launched. Synology’s DSM 7.3 announcement says 25-series Plus, Value and J models accept non-validated third-party drives for storage pools, so the WD drives above work. Where it falls short:
 Plex transcoding needs a workaround: the DS225+ ships without the i915 modules Plex and Jellyfin use, and the fix is the community Transcode for x25 package .
 No M.2 slots: an SSD cache would cost one of your two drive bays.
 An old CPU: the J4125 dates from 2019, and 6 GB is the RAM ceiling for its whole life.
 Pick it if backups, photo sync and file shares are the job and you want software that needs no tinkering, at about $365 sold by Amazon.com. Look elsewhere if Plex is part of the plan, because running an unofficial driver package on your only copy of the family photos is the opposite of why you’d buy a Synology in the first place.
 Check DS225+ price on Amazon 
 2. UGREEN DXP2800
 For a 2-bay Plex or Jellyfin server, the DXP2800 is the standout. Its Intel N100 has Quick Sync and it ships with 8 GB of DDR5, four times the RAM of the DS225+. It also has the two M.2 slots the Synology lacks, for about $25 more.
 UGREEN NASync DXP2800: Intel N100, 8 GB DDR5, two NVMe slots, 2.5GbE. Image: UGREEN. 
 Intel’s N100 is a four-core chip, and Quick Sync is the transcoding path Plex and Jellyfin support best. That is why this box handles media without any driver workarounds. The RAM sits in one SO-DIMM slot that takes 16 GB, and the network is one 2.5GbE port. The OS boots from a 32 GB eMMC chip, so both bays stay free for data. ocinside measured about 7 W idle , 34.7 W at peak, and 181 MB/s writing to a RAID 1 pair.
 UGREEN’s software, UGOS Pro, is younger than DSM, and you will notice it in the backup and photo apps more than in file sharing. What you give up:
 Noise: UGREEN rates it at 29 to 34 dB in quiet mode, higher than the 19.6 dB(A) Synology quotes for the DS225+, though the two are measured differently.
 Warranty: two years against Synology’s three.
 M.2 speed: the N100 platform runs PCIe Gen 3, so the NVMe slots won’t run Gen 4 drives at full speed.
 It’s also the box that grows with you. In a March 2024 update to NASCompares’ UGREEN Q&A , a UGREEN representative said the warranty covers only the hardware and warned that a third-party OS risks data loss and compatibility issues, though older text on that page still says it voids the warranty. TrueNAS or Unraid later is an option, but get UGREEN’s answer in writing first. Pick it at about $390, sold by UGREEN, if Plex is on the plan. For more media-server boxes beyond two bays, see our NAS picks for Plex and self-hosting .
 Check DXP2800 price on Amazon 
 3. TerraMaster F2-425
 The F2-425 is the cheapest way into an x86 NAS with Quick Sync, at about $255, which is $135 less than the DXP2800 and only $45 more than the ARM-based DS223j. TerraMaster rates its Celeron N5095 for H.264 and H.265 transcoding at 4K60.
 TerraMaster F2-425: Celeron N5095, 4 GB RAM up to 16 GB, 2.5GbE. Image: TerraMaster. 
 You get 4 GB of RAM in a SODIMM slot that takes 16 GB, one 2.5GbE port, two 10Gbps USB ports and HDMI, and bays for up to 60 TB raw. TerraMaster’s product page title says N95 while its spec table says N5095; we’ve gone with the spec table, and so should you when comparing. TerraMaster rates it at 22 W working and 11 W in hibernation, the highest hibernation figure of the budget picks.
 Its low price comes with three conditions you should accept up front:
 The OS is locked: TerraMaster states that installing another system voids the warranty , so this box runs TOS for its whole life.
 An older chip: the N5095 is a 2021 Jasper Lake part, and there is no M.2 slot for a cache.
 Thin stock: Amazon showed 9 units left from TerraMaster’s storefront when we checked.
 Buy it if you want Plex-capable hardware on the smallest budget and you’re happy with TerraMaster’s own software. If the price climbs back toward its $300 list, the DXP2800 is the better buy for the extra RAM and M.2 slots.
 Check F2-425 price on Amazon 
 4. UGREEN DXP2800 GT
 The GT is the 2-bay NAS for a home that already has 10GbE, or plans to. It’s the only box here with a 10GbE port, and its two SO-DIMM slots take up to 64 GB, enough for real VMs next to the file shares.
 UGREEN NASync DXP2800 GT: Ryzen Embedded R2514, 10GbE, up to 64 GB RAM. Image: UGREEN. 
 It runs an AMD Ryzen Embedded R2514 with four cores and eight threads at up to 3.7 GHz, ships with 8 GB of DDR4, and has two NVMe slots. The bays also take U.2 drives. Notebookcheck measured 14.84 to 20.14 W idle, 35.9 W at peak, and 29.11 dB(A) idle at 30 cm, and called it surprisingly quiet. One spec doesn’t match the price, though:
 No Quick Sync: the Radeon graphics are not Intel’s encoder, so check your media server’s AMD support before you count on transcoding.
 Power: UGREEN rates it at 42.36 W working and 18.12 W in hibernation, about two and a half times the DXP2800.
 M.2 lanes: Mighty Gadget reports each NVMe slot runs at Gen 3 x2.
 Two bays and 10GbE is an odd pairing, because a mirrored pair of hard drives cannot fill a 10GbE link on its own. The port earns its keep when you put fast NVMe storage in those slots. Pick it at about $460, sold by UGREEN, if you will use the NVMe slots and the RAM; for a plain backup box it’s paying for hardware you’ll never touch.
 Check DXP2800 GT price on Amazon 
 5. Synology DS223j
 If all you want is a place for laptop and phone backups with Synology’s software, the DS223j does it for about $210. It runs the same DSM as the DS225+, including Btrfs, Synology Hybrid RAID and snapshot replication.
 Synology DS223j: Realtek ARM chip, 1 GB RAM, one 1GbE port. Image: Synology. 
 Synology kept the hardware minimal on purpose: a four-core Realtek RTD1619B ARM chip at 1.7 GHz, 1 GB of RAM that cannot be upgraded, and one 1GbE port. StorageReview measured 115 MB/s reads and writes over SMB in RAID 1, which is gigabit line rate, so the drives were never the bottleneck. Synology’s own spec table suggests a ceiling of 5 users in Synology Drive.
 The bays are not hot-swap, so a failed drive means powering the box down before you swap it. The warranty is two years, not three, and there is no Intel Quick Sync, so plan on direct play rather than transcoding. It’s quiet at 18.2 dB(A) and rated at 4 W in hibernation. Buy it as a backup target and nothing more; if you can stretch to the F2-425 for $45 extra, you get x86, Quick Sync and 2.5GbE.
 Check DS223j price on Amazon 
 6. UGREEN DH2300
 Of the six, the DH2300 draws the least power, rated at 13.72 W working and 3.3 W in hibernation, which makes it the cheapest box here to leave on. UGREEN sells it as a beginner’s backup NAS, and it’s honest about the limits.
 UGREEN NASync DH2300: eight-core Rockchip ARM, 4 GB RAM, 1GbE. Image: UGREEN. 
 It pairs an eight-core Rockchip chip (an RK3576, per PCMag’s review ) with 4 GB of RAM, one 1GbE port and bays for up to 64 TB. PCMag measured 107 MB/s writes and 108 MB/s reads, gigabit speed again. UGREEN’s own product page tells you not to buy it for a Plex server or Home Assistant, and there’s no Docker and no VM support. The apps UGREEN ships are the apps you get.
 Against the DS223j, you trade DSM for four times the RAM and a lower power rating, and you pay about $29 more. Stock was thin, with 12 units left from UGREEN’s storefront when we checked. Pick it for a quiet backup box that stays on, at about $239, and pick the DS223j instead if you want Synology’s backup apps.
 Check DH2300 price on Amazon 
 What a 2-bay NAS costs to run for a year
 A home NAS stays on around the clock, so the power rating is a running cost you’ll pay every month. We took each maker’s “access” figure, which is measured with drives working, and ran it for all 8,760 hours of a year at $0.20 per kWh. Scale the last column to your own rate:
 Model Rated access power Rated hibernation kWh per year at access Cost per year at $0.20/kWh 
 UGREEN DH2300 13.72 W 3.30 W 120.2 $24.04 
 Synology DS223j 16.31 W 4.00 W 142.9 $28.58 
 UGREEN DXP2800 16.38 W 5.24 W 143.5 $28.70 
 Synology DS225+ 16.98 W 6.08 W 148.7 $29.75 
 TerraMaster F2-425 22.00 W 11.00 W 192.7 $38.54 
 UGREEN DXP2800 GT 42.36 W 18.12 W 371.1 $74.21 
 Treat these numbers as a worst case. A home NAS spends most of its day idle or with drives spun down, and the reviews above measured lower idle figures than these ratings. Even so, the gap is the useful part. Four of the six cost $24 to $30 a year to run, so power shouldn’t decide between them. The GT costs about $45 a year more than the DXP2800, which adds up to about $228 over five years, three times the $70 gap in their prices.
 What first-time NAS owners should check before buying
 Most first-NAS regrets come from a handful of assumptions that sound reasonable and aren’t. Go through these before you order:
 RAID 1 is not a backup: a mirror survives one dead drive, but a deleted file, ransomware or a fire takes out both copies at once. Keep a second copy off the NAS, on a USB drive or a cloud bucket.
 Two bays means one drive of space: plan capacity for three or four years, because the only way to grow is replacing both drives.
 Plex needs Quick Sync: phones and smart TVs often can’t play every file directly, and without a hardware encoder the NAS can’t convert it on the fly. Since DSM 7.2.2, Synology Photos and its other media apps hand HEVC, AVC and VC-1 to the playing device instead of converting them.
 Gigabit caps copy speed: 1GbE boxes top out near 115 MB/s, which is fine for backups and a bottleneck for editing video off the NAS.
 The OS is part of the purchase: TerraMaster voids the warranty on a third-party OS, Synology runs only DSM, and UGREEN has warned of data-loss risk with a third-party OS.
 Buy CMR drives: SMR drives can turn a routine rebuild into a multi-day crawl, and a 2-bay box has no second parity to fall back on while it runs.
 People skip the first item most often. If the off-NAS copy is a USB disk, our list of external drives for backups covers which ones hold up. The NAS’s own backup app can write to it on a schedule.
 Models left out on purpose
 A few popular 2-bay boxes didn’t make the cut, and the reasons are about buying them, not about the hardware:
 QNAP TS-264: listed at about $469, but the only seller was Adorama with thin stock, and at that price the DXP2800 GT adds 10GbE.
 TerraMaster F2-425 Plus: about $425, but we couldn’t confirm which CPU ships on the current listing, since N150 and N95 versions both exist.
 Four bays: if you want RAID 5 or room to add drives later, our 4-bay NAS guide prices that step up.
 If you’re leaving Synology rather than starting fresh, the Synology alternatives roundup compares the same UGREEN boxes against QNAP, UniFi and DIY builds.
 Where each 2-bay NAS falls short
 No box here is right for every home, so it helps to know the single weakness you’d live with on each:
 Synology DS225+: Plex transcoding needs an unofficial driver package, and RAM stops at 6 GB.
 UGREEN DXP2800: louder than the Synologys, with younger software and a two-year warranty.
 TerraMaster F2-425: any other OS voids the warranty, and stock was down to single digits.
 UGREEN DXP2800 GT: no Quick Sync and the highest power draw. Its 10GbE port is also wasted on a pair of hard drives alone.
 Synology DS223j: 1 GB of fixed RAM, gigabit only, and no hot-swap bays.
 UGREEN DH2300: no Docker, no VMs and no Plex server, by UGREEN’s own description.
 For most first-time owners we’d still start with the DS225+ for backups or the DXP2800 for media, because their weaknesses are the easiest to live with. Whichever you pick, spend the money you save on the box on the biggest CMR pair you can afford, since that’s the part you can’t upgrade without starting over.

Best Budget NAS and Cheapest NAS Setups for 2026 | Starry Hope Starry Hope 
 The Best Budget NAS in 2026, Priced With Two Drives
Updated on
 November 2, 2026,
by Jim Mendenhall 
 Bottom line 
 The UGREEN DXP2800 is our budget NAS pick for most homes that want Plex, photo backup, and a few apps. It costs a little more than the cheapest two-bay boxes, and it adds two SSD slots and a faster network port. A household that only needs backups can save money with the cheaper UGREEN DH2300.
Recommendation
 Pair the DXP2800 with two 8TB NAS drives if the budget allows, since two 4TB drives cost less but fill up sooner.
 The UGREEN DXP2800 is our pick for most homes on a budget, and with two NAS hard drives the whole setup costs about $770 to $1,110. Two drives are the smallest setup that survives a drive failure, so every total below includes them. Hard drive prices roughly doubled over the past two years, and a pair of 4TB NAS drives now costs about as much as the DXP2800 itself. That shrinks what the cheaper boxes save. The DXP2800 adds $120 to $150 to the total over the cheapest two-bay setup, and the money buys a faster network port, an Intel chip that transcodes video, and two SSD slots.
 Every price below is a maker’s list or store price for the box, plus a rounded range for the drives as of October 2026. Drive prices move by tens of dollars from week to week.
 What the cheapest NAS setups cost with two drives
 The table pairs each box with two 4TB NAS drives (about $380 to $480 for the pair) and two 8TB NAS drives (about $660 to $720). In RAID 1, the mirror layout for two drives, two 4TB drives give you 4TB of usable space and two 8TB drives give you 8TB, because every file is written to both drives.
 Box Bays Box price With two 4TB drives With two 8TB drives 
 UGREEN DH2300 2 $269.99 list, $239.99 on sale about $620 to $750 about $900 to $990 
 TerraMaster F2-425 2 $299.99 list, $254.99 on sale about $635 to $780 about $915 to $1,020 
 UGREEN DXP2800 2 $389.99 (marked down from $439.99) about $770 to $870 about $1,050 to $1,110 
 TerraMaster F4-425 Plus (N95) 4 $599.99 about $980 to $1,080 about $1,260 to $1,320 
 UGREEN DXP4800 GT 4 $659.99 about $1,040 to $1,140 about $1,320 to $1,380 
 The lowest total on the list is about $620, and that buys 4TB of mirrored storage on a box with a 1GbE port, 4GB of fixed RAM, and no official Docker support. The DXP2800 setup costs about $120 to $150 more and gives the same 4TB with a 2.5GbE port, a chip that runs Plex and Docker, and two M.2 SSD slots. With 8TB drives the gap between those two setups stays the same in dollars and shrinks as a share of the total.
 The two four-bay boxes in the table cost $210 to $270 more than the DXP2800 and do not need all four drives on day one. Two drives in a four-bay box leave two empty bays for later, which matters more now that the cheapest way to add space is to add a drive rather than replace both.
 Our budget pick is the UGREEN DXP2800
 UGREEN NASync DXP2800
 Editor's Choice 
 2-Bay 2.5GbE 8GB RAM Intel Processor N100 
 List price $389.99 | Full specs 
Check Price on Amazon
 The UGREEN DXP2800 costs $389.99 on UGREEN’s store, marked down from $439.99, and runs on an Intel N100, a four-core chip from 2023 with Intel Quick Sync, the video engine that lets Plex or Jellyfin convert a 4K movie for a phone or an older TV without loading the CPU. It ships with 8GB of DDR5 in one slot (16GB maximum), a 2.5GbE port, two M.2 NVMe slots, and tool-less 3.5-inch trays in a metal case. A 2.5GbE port moves about 280 MB/s, close to the 300 MB/s that TechRadar gives as the practical ceiling for two hard drives striped together. A 1GbE port tops out near 115 MB/s.
 UGREEN’s UGOS Pro software includes a Docker app, so Immich, Home Assistant, or Pi-hole can run next to the file shares. The M.2 slots take an SSD cache or a separate SSD pool for those apps. UGREEN also lets you install TrueNAS or Unraid without voiding the warranty, so you can switch systems later without buying new hardware. OCinside measured about 7 W at idle in its December 2024 review , so the box itself costs about $10 a year to run at 17 cents per kWh; two spinning drives add more, and our 24/7 power cost math covers how to price that at your local rate.
 Two bays mean RAID 1 or RAID 0 only, so growing past two drives means replacing both with larger ones. There is no PCIe slot, so the only route past 2.5GbE is a USB network adapter. UGOS Pro has fewer apps than Synology’s DSM, and Plex and Jellyfin install as Docker containers rather than one-click packages. How-To Geek’s review of a pre-release unit in April 2024 said UGOS “needs a lot of work”; Docker and most of the missing features arrived in later updates, and Macworld’s July 2025 review called the interface intuitive but found UGOS Pro less mature than Synology’s and QNAP’s systems.
 The UGREEN DH2300 is the cheapest box and suits backups only
 The UGREEN DH2300 launched in 2025 at $209.99, and in October 2026 UGREEN’s store lists it at $269.99, on sale for $239.99. It runs UGOS Pro on a Rockchip RK3576, an eight-core ARM chip, with 4GB of RAM soldered to the board and a single 1GbE port. TechRadar’s November 2025 review by Mark Pickavance gave it 4.5 out of 5 and called it “a terrific NAS that does most of what these things are bought for, without breaking the bank.”
 It handles phone photo backup, a shared folder, and nightly PC backups. TechRadar measured 118 MB/s over the built-in 1GbE port with two 4TB IronWolf drives. With a USB 2.5GbE adapter (about $25), reads rose to 296 MB/s and writes to 286 MB/s. TechRadar also found that a cheap SATA SSD can act as a read cache for a single hard drive.
 The RAM cannot be upgraded, and UGREEN’s product page says the DH2300 does not have official Docker support or virtual machines. TechRadar wrote that with 4GB “it can only handle a couple of major Docker containers.” The ARM chip cannot run Windows or Linux virtual machines, and there are no M.2 slots. Even with a $25 USB 2.5GbE adapter, the DH2300 setup costs about $95 to $125 less than a DXP2800 setup, about 11% to 16% of the DXP2800 setup’s total with 4TB drives.
 The TerraMaster F2-425 is the cheapest Intel two-bay
 The TerraMaster F2-425 sits between the two UGREEN boxes. It pairs an Intel Celeron N5095 from 2021 with 4GB of DDR4 (16GB maximum), a 2.5GbE port, and TerraMaster’s TOS software, and TerraMaster’s store lists it at $299.99 with sales to about $255. Because it is an Intel chip, it runs Docker and virtual machines and has Quick Sync for video transcoding. PCWorld’s October 2025 review by Jon L. Jacobi called it “a good value for streaming media over your home network, handling IP cams, and backing up your computer,” and listed “occasional interface rough spots” and an “all-plastic case” as its cons.
 It has no M.2 slots, and its chip is two years older than the N100 in the DXP2800. At sale prices it is about $135 below the DXP2800. That buys Plex and a couple of containers if you can do without SSD slots. At its $299.99 list price the gap to the DXP2800 shrinks to $90, and the DXP2800 is the better use of that money.
 Four-bay boxes leave room for two more drives
 TerraMaster F4-425 Plus
 Most Expandable 
 4-Bay 5GbE 8GB RAM Intel Processor N95 
 List price $599.99 | Full specs 
Check Price on Amazon
 UGREEN NASync DXP4800 GT
 Best Performance 
 4-Bay 10GbE 8GB RAM AMD Ryzen Embedded R2514 
 List price $659.99 | Full specs 
Check Price on Amazon
 A two-bay NAS has one upgrade path: replace both drives with larger ones and copy the data across. A four-bay box lets you start with two drives in RAID 1 and add two more later, or move to RAID 5, where one drive’s worth of space protects the rest. If your photo and video library keeps growing, adding drives to empty bays avoids retiring a working pair of drives. Our NAS comparison chart treats four bays as the practical starting point for a home NAS, and that holds for anyone who can see past 8TB. On a tight budget, a two-bay box is the cheaper entry.
 Close modal 
 The TerraMaster F4-425 Plus in its Intel N95 version lists at $599.99 with 8GB of DDR4, three M.2 NVMe slots, and two 5GbE ports, which is faster networking than any other box in this guide except the DXP4800 GT. The N95 is a 2023 chip in the same class as the DXP2800’s N100, with Quick Sync. The cons are a single RAM slot, M.2 slots that each run at one PCIe lane, and no PCIe slot for a 10GbE card.
 The UGREEN DXP4800 GT lists at $659.99 and moves to an AMD Ryzen Embedded R2514 with two 10GbE ports and ECC memory support. It is the only box here with 10GbE, which only pays off if your PC and switch also have 10GbE. It transcodes H.264 and H.265 video, but PCWorld’s review measured about 25 W with the drives asleep, so it costs more to run around the clock than the Intel N-series boxes.
 For tinkerers there is also the AOOSTAR WTR PRO 5825U , a four-bay barebone at $379 with an eight-core Ryzen 7 5825U and dual 2.5GbE. It ships with no RAM, no SSD, and no NAS software, so the full cost is $379 plus a DDR4 kit and a boot SSD, plus an evening installing TrueNAS or Unraid. The bays are not hot-swappable, so you power it down to change a drive. It is a poor fit for anyone who wants a setup wizard.
 Drive prices doubled, and small drives cost the most per terabyte
 Close modal 
 The NASDisks price tracker reports that the typical NAS hard drive of 8TB and up went from $21 per terabyte in July 2024 to $47 per terabyte in October 2026, more than double. MakeUseOf’s September 2026 report traces the cause to data center demand: “Western Digital says it’s sold out of nearline hard drive capacity through calendar 2026.” Analysts cited in that report do not expect prices to normalize before late 2027, so waiting for a sale is a weak plan.
 At the cheaper end of each size, a 4TB NAS drive costs roughly $48 to $60 per terabyte, an 8TB drive about $41 to $45, and 12TB drives fall to about $36. The 4TB pair is still the lowest total outlay. If you can spend about $250 more, the 8TB pair doubles your usable space for about 60% more on the drives.
 The drives to look for are CMR models sold for NAS use, such as WD Red Plus, Seagate IronWolf, or Toshiba N300. CMR (conventional magnetic recording) drives handle the long rebuild a RAID mirror runs after a drive swap. Plain WD Red drives (without “Plus”) in the 2TB to 6TB range use SMR (shingled magnetic recording), which writes slowly under sustained load and can stretch a rebuild into days. Recertified enterprise drives were the budget trick of 2024 and 2025, and they no longer help much. PC Server and Parts tracked a recertified 24TB Seagate Exos going from $298.99 to $699 in a year.
 SSD prices rose too. NASCompares’ July 2026 roundup shows 4TB NVMe SSDs that sold for about $190 to $230 in June 2025 listed at about $699 to $900 or more. At those prices, an all-SSD NAS costs far more per terabyte than one with hard drives.
 Where Synology and a mini PC fit
 Synology’s cheapest two-bay, the DS223j, runs Synology’s DSM software on a Realtek RTD1619B with 1GB of RAM and a 1GbE port. When TechRadar reviewed the DH2300 at its $209.99 launch price, it noted the DS223j cost “a few dollars less” and had a weaker chip and a quarter of the memory. Its draw is DSM’s backup apps, such as Hyper Backup and Snapshot Replication. Synology’s two-bay DS225+ starts near $400, the same price as a DXP2800, with a 2019 Celeron and 2GB of RAM; see our UGREEN vs Synology comparison for that matchup.
 A used office mini PC with TrueNAS or Unraid is cheaper still for the box: off-lease Dell OptiPlex and Lenovo ThinkCentre Micro models sell for $100 to $200. They hold one or two internal drives, have 1GbE, and need a USB enclosure for more disks, which is a weaker setup for a RAID mirror than a NAS with dedicated drive bays. Our guide to using a mini PC as a NAS covers that route, including the Beelink ME Mini , a small box with six M.2 SSD slots. The ME Mini was a cheap NAS in 2025, but with 4TB SSDs now costing several times a 4TB hard drive, it has become a pricey way to buy capacity.
 Which budget setup to buy
 For most homes, the setup we would choose is the UGREEN DXP2800 with two 8TB NAS drives, at roughly $1,050 to $1,110. If that is too much, two 4TB drives bring the total down to roughly $770 to $870 and still give you a working mirror. Nothing cheaper in this guide pairs Quick Sync video transcoding and Docker with SSD slots and a 2.5GbE port.
 Someone who only wants a home for backups and shared files can spend less. The UGREEN DH2300 with two 4TB drives comes to about $620 to $750, and a $25 USB 2.5GbE adapter is worth adding if your PC has a 2.5GbE port. If your files could outgrow 8TB within a few years, the TerraMaster F4-425 Plus N95 model with two drives makes more sense, because adding two drives later costs less than replacing both drives in a two-bay box.
 Whatever you buy, a RAID 1 mirror protects you from a dead drive, not from a deleted folder, ransomware, or a house fire. Keep a second copy of the files you cannot replace on a USB drive or a cloud backup service.
